topics.title: Lower Extremity Arterial Anatomy
topics.content:
The arterial system of the lower extremity begins with the common femoral artery (CFA), which bifurcates into the superficial femoral artery (SFA) and profunda femoris (deep femoral artery).

Key Points:
• CFA is located at the inguinal ligament
• SFA continues to become the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus
• Profunda femoris supplies the thigh muscles
• Popliteal artery trifurcates into anterior tibial, posterior tibial, and peroneal arteries

topics.title: Lower Extremity Venous Anatomy
topics.content:
The venous system consists of deep veins, superficial veins, and perforating veins that connect them.

Deep Venous System:
• Follows the arterial system
• Common femoral vein (CFV)
• Femoral vein (FV)
• Popliteal vein
• Tibial veins (anterior, posterior)
• Peroneal veins

Superficial Venous System:
• Great saphenous vein (GSV) - longest vein in the body
• Small saphenous vein (SSV)
• Saphenofemoral junction (SFJ)
• Saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ)

Perforating Veins:
• Connect superficial to deep system
• Cockett perforators
• Boyd perforator
• Dodd perforator

topics.title: Carotid & Cerebrovascular Anatomy
topics.content:
The carotid system supplies blood to the brain and face.

Key Structures:
• Common carotid artery (CCA) - no branches
• Internal carotid artery (ICA) - no extracranial branches
• External carotid artery (ECA) - multiple branches
• Carotid bulb - at the bifurcation, area of low resistance

ICA Characteristics:
• Larger diameter than ECA
• Low resistance waveform
• Posterolateral position
• No extracranial branches

ECA Characteristics:
• Smaller diameter
• High resistance waveform
• Anteromedial position
• Multiple branches (superior thyroid, lingual, facial, etc.)

Circle of Willis:
• Provides collateral circulation to the brain
• Connects ICA and vertebrobasilar systems

topics.title: Basic Flow Principles
topics.content:
Understanding blood flow dynamics is essential for vascular interpretation.

Key Concepts:

Laminar Flow:
• Normal flow pattern
• Parabolic velocity profile
• Fastest flow in center
• Slower flow near vessel walls

Turbulent Flow:
• Chaotic, disorganized flow
• Occurs with stenosis, post-stenotic, or high velocities
• Creates spectral broadening on Doppler

Reynolds Number:
• Predicts laminar vs turbulent flow
• >2000 = turbulent flow likely
• Factors: velocity, diameter, density, viscosity

Poiseuille's Law:
• Flow = (ΔP × π × r⁴) / (8 × η × L)
• Flow is proportional to radius to the 4th power
• Small changes in diameter dramatically affect flow

topics.title: Doppler Waveform Analysis
topics.content:
Arterial Waveforms:

Triphasic (Normal):
• Forward flow (systole)
• Reverse flow (early diastole)
• Forward flow (late diastole)
• Indicates normal resistance, no proximal stenosis

Biphasic:
• Forward flow, reverse flow
• May be normal variant or mild disease

Monophasic:
• Forward flow only
• Indicates high resistance or proximal stenosis
• Loss of reverse flow component

Venous Waveforms:

Phasic:
• Flow varies with respiration
• Normal in periphery

Pulsatile:
• Flow varies with cardiac cycle
• Normal near heart (IVC, iliac veins)
• Abnormal in extremities (suggests CHF, tricuspid regurgitation)

Continuous/Non-phasic:
• Constant flow, no variation
• Abnormal - suggests proximal obstruction

topics.title: Doppler Equation & Principles
topics.content:
The Doppler Effect:
• Change in frequency when sound reflects off moving object
• Basis for measuring blood flow velocity

Doppler Equation:
ΔF = (2 × F₀ × V × cos θ) / C

Where:
• ΔF = Doppler shift frequency
• F₀ = transmitted frequency
• V = blood velocity
• θ = Doppler angle
• C = speed of sound in tissue (1540 m/s)

Angle Correction:
• Doppler angle should be <60°
• Best angle: 45-60°
• 0° = no Doppler shift (perpendicular)
• 90° = maximum shift (parallel)
• As angle increases, accuracy decreases

Spectral Doppler Parameters:
• Peak Systolic Velocity (PSV)
• End Diastolic Velocity (EDV)
• Resistive Index (RI) = (PSV - EDV) / PSV
• Pulsatility Index (PI) = (PSV - EDV) / mean velocity

topics.title: Arterial Stenosis & Occlusion
topics.content:
Arterial narrowing due to atherosclerosis, most common vascular pathology.

Stenosis Grading Criteria:

Carotid ICA Stenosis (NASCET):
• Normal: PSV <125 cm/s, no plaque
• <50%: PSV <125 cm/s, plaque present
• 50-69%: PSV 125-230 cm/s, ICA/CCA ratio <2.0
• 70-99%: PSV >230 cm/s, ICA/CCA ratio >4.0
• Occlusion: No flow

Peripheral Arterial Stenosis:
• <50%: PSV ratio <2.0
• 50-75%: PSV ratio 2.0-4.0
• >75%: PSV ratio >4.0
• Critical: Monophasic waveform, low velocities

Signs of Stenosis:
• Elevated PSV at stenosis
• Turbulent flow
• Spectral broadening
• Post-stenotic turbulence
• Aliasing on color Doppler
• Dampened waveform distally

topics.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
topics.content:
Blood clot in the deep venous system.

Diagnostic Criteria:
• Non-compressibility (PRIMARY criterion)
• Visible thrombus on B-mode
• Absent or diminished color flow
• Absent or abnormal Doppler signal
• Vein distension
• Loss of phasicity

Acute vs Chronic DVT:

Acute DVT:
• Hypoechoic/anechoic thrombus
• Distended vein
• Non-compressible
• May see free-floating thrombus

Chronic DVT:
• Echogenic (bright) thrombus
• Vein may be small/scarred
• Thickened vein walls
• Possible recanalization
• Collateral vessels present

Compression Technique:
• Apply gentle pressure every 1-2 cm
• Vein walls should coapt completely
• Any separation = thrombus
• Scan CFV, FV, popliteal, tibial veins

topics.title: Chronic Venous Insufficiency
topics.content:
Incompetent venous valves causing reflux (reverse flow).

Reflux Testing:
• Patient standing or reverse Trendelenburg
• Distal augmentation (calf squeeze)
• Measure reflux duration
• >0.5 sec = abnormal (superficial veins)
• >1.0 sec = abnormal (deep veins)

Common Sites:
• GSV (most common)
• SSV
• Perforating veins
• Deep veins (less common)

Signs & Symptoms:
• Varicose veins
• Leg swelling
• Skin changes (hemosiderin staining)
• Venous ulcers
• Pain, heaviness

Treatment Considerations:
• Compression therapy
• Ablation (RF, laser)
• Sclerotherapy
• Surgical stripping
• Perforator ligation

topics.title: Aneurysms
topics.content:
Localized dilation of a vessel, typically >50% increase in diameter.

Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):
• Normal aorta: <3 cm
• Ectatic: 3.0-3.9 cm
• Aneurysm: ≥3.0 cm (some use ≥3.5 cm)
• Large: ≥5.0 cm
• Surgical repair considered at 5.5 cm

Types:
• True aneurysm: All 3 vessel layers intact
• False aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm): Contained rupture, hematoma
• Fusiform: Circumferential dilation
• Saccular: Localized outpouching

Popliteal Artery Aneurysm:
• ≥0.7 cm or >1.5× normal diameter
• Risk of thrombosis and embolization
• Associated with AAA in 50% of cases

Pseudoaneurysm:
• Post-catheterization complication
• "Yin-yang" sign on color Doppler
• To-and-fro waveform in neck
• May spontaneously thrombose
• Ultrasound-guided compression treatment

topics.title: Carotid Duplex Protocol
topics.content:
Standard protocol for evaluating extracranial carotid arteries.

Patient Position:
• Supine, head slightly extended
• Turn head away from side being scanned
• Pillow under shoulders if needed

Transducer:
• Linear array, 5-12 MHz
• Lower frequency for deeper vessels

B-Mode Imaging:
• Longitudinal and transverse views
• CCA (proximal, mid, distal)
• Carotid bulb
• ICA (proximal, mid, distal)
• ECA (proximal)
• Vertebral artery origin and V2 segment

Color Doppler:
• Identify areas of stenosis (aliasing, turbulence)
• Evaluate plaque morphology
• Confirm vessel patency

Spectral Doppler:
• Angle <60°
• Sample volume 1.5-2 mm
• Wall filter appropriate
• Velocities at each segment:
  - Proximal CCA
  - Mid CCA
  - Distal CCA
  - Carotid bulb
  - Proximal ICA
  - Mid ICA
  - Distal ICA
  - Proximal ECA
  - Vertebral artery

Key Measurements:
• ICA PSV and EDV
• CCA PSV and EDV
• ICA/CCA ratio
• Plaque location and characteristics

topics.title: Lower Extremity Arterial Protocol
topics.content:
Complete arterial evaluation from aorta to foot.

Patient Position:
• Supine for anterior approach
• Prone or lateral for popliteal artery

Transducer:
• Linear 5-12 MHz for superficial vessels
• Curved 2-5 MHz for iliac arteries

Segments to Evaluate:
1. Distal aorta
2. Common iliac arteries
3. External iliac arteries
4. Common femoral artery
5. Profunda femoris
6. Superficial femoral artery
7. Popliteal artery
8. Anterior tibial artery
9. Posterior tibial artery
10. Peroneal artery
11. Dorsalis pedis
12. Posterior tibial at ankle

For Each Segment:
• B-mode imaging (longitudinal/transverse)
• Color Doppler for flow direction
• Spectral Doppler with angle correction
• Document PSV at stenosis
• Assess waveform characteristics

Stenosis Assessment:
• Velocity ratios (PSV ratio >2.0)
• Waveform changes (monophasic)
• Color aliasing
• Post-stenotic turbulence
• Distal dampening

ABI (Ankle-Brachial Index):
• Normal: 1.0-1.3
• Mild disease: 0.9-0.99
• Moderate: 0.5-0.89
• Severe: <0.5

topics.title: DVT Examination Protocol
topics.content:
Standard compression ultrasound for DVT evaluation.

Patient Position:
• Supine, leg externally rotated
• Knee slightly bent
• Reverse Trendelenburg to distend veins

Transducer:
• Linear array, 5-12 MHz
• Lower frequency for obese patients

Compression Technique:
• Apply gentle, firm pressure
• Compress every 1-2 cm along vein
• Normal vein completely collapses
• Any residual lumen = thrombus

Complete Exam:
1. Common femoral vein (CFV)
2. Saphenofemoral junction (SFJ)
3. Femoral vein (FV)
4. Deep femoral vein (DFV)
5. Popliteal vein
6. Posterior tibial veins
7. Peroneal veins
8. Anterior tibial veins (if indicated)

For Each Segment:
• B-mode imaging (transverse primarily)
• Compression every 1-2 cm
• Color Doppler to confirm flow
• Spectral Doppler:
  - Phasicity with respiration
  - Augmentation with distal compression
  - Competent valves

Signs of DVT:
• Non-compressibility (PRIMARY)
• Visible thrombus
• Absent color flow
• Absent/abnormal Doppler signal
• Loss of phasicity
• Vein distension

Documentation:
• Cine clip of compression (positive/negative)
• Color Doppler images
• Spectral Doppler waveforms
• Measurements of thrombus if present

topics.title: Basic Ultrasound Physics
topics.content:
Fundamental principles of diagnostic ultrasound.

Sound Wave Properties:
• Frequency: cycles per second (Hz)
• Wavelength: distance of one cycle
• Velocity: speed of sound through medium
• Amplitude: strength of wave

Relationship:
Velocity = Frequency × Wavelength
C = f × λ

Speed of Sound:
• Soft tissue average: 1540 m/s
• Air: 330 m/s
• Bone: 4080 m/s
• Fat: 1450 m/s
• Blood: 1560 m/s

Frequency Ranges:
• Diagnostic ultrasound: 2-20 MHz
• Vascular imaging: typically 5-12 MHz
• Deeper structures: lower frequency
• Superficial structures: higher frequency

Penetration vs Resolution:
• Higher frequency = better resolution, less penetration
• Lower frequency = better penetration, less resolution
• Must balance based on depth of interest

topics.title: Ultrasound Artifacts
topics.content:
Common artifacts encountered in vascular imaging.

Mirror Image:
• Strong reflector creates duplicate image
• Common with diaphragm, pleura
• Appears on opposite side of reflector

Shadowing:
• Acoustic shadow behind highly attenuating structure
• Calcified plaque creates shadowing
• Prevents visualization of structures behind

Enhancement:
• Increased echoes behind fluid-filled structure
• Through-transmission
• Helps identify cystic structures

Reverberation:
• Multiple reflections between two surfaces
• Appears as equally spaced lines
• Common with air, foreign bodies

Aliasing:
• Color Doppler artifact
• Velocities exceed Nyquist limit
• Color reversal (appears to flow opposite direction)
• Fix by: increasing scale (PRF), using lower frequency, or continuous wave Doppler

Spectral Broadening:
• Filling in of spectral window
• Can indicate turbulent flow/stenosis
• Also caused by large sample volume

Twinkling Artifact:
• Color Doppler behind calcification
• Appears as rapid color changes
• Helps identify calculi, calcification
